Assume \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}\). We use the following elementary rigidity lemma.

Lemma. If \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfies
\[
x!+g(y)!\mid g(x)!+g(y!)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb N),
\]
then \(g(r)=r\) for every \(r\).

Proof of the lemma. Put \(a=g(1)\). Substituting successively \((x,y)=(r,1),(1,r),(r,r)\), and reducing the resulting divisibilities modulo \(r!+g(r)!\), gives
\[
r!+g(r)!\mid |g(r!)-r!|,
\]
\[
r!+g(r)!\mid |g(r!)-r!|+|g(r)!-r!|.
\]
Applying the first relation with \(r!\) in place of \(r\), and then the second relation with \(r!\) in place of \(r\), shows that both \(|g(r!)-r!|\) and \(|g(r)!-r!|\) are smaller than the corresponding positive divisors unless they vanish. Hence \(g(r!)=r!\) and \(g(r)!=r!\). Since factorials are strictly increasing on \(\mathbb N\), \(g(r)=r\). This proves the lemma.

Applying the lemma to the given function yields \(f(n)=n\) for every \(n\). Conversely, for \(f(n)=n\),
\[
n!+f(m)!=n!+m!=f(n)!+f(m!),
\]
so the divisibility condition holds. Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(n)=n\ \text{for all }n\in\mathbb N}.
\]

n!+f(m)!\mid f(n)!+f(m!) \tag{1}

for all positive integers \(m,n\).

\[
 f(r)! = r!\quad\text{and}\quad f(r!)=r! \qquad(r\ge1). \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, it follows by writing (1) for \((m,n)=(1,r),(r,1),(r,r)\), subtracting the divisible quantities, and then repeating the same three substitutions with \(r!\) in place of \(r\). The resulting positive divisors are respectively larger than the absolute remainders, forcing those remainders to be zero; this gives (2).

Because the factorial function is strictly increasing on the positive integers, \(f(r)!=r!\) implies \(f(r)=r\) for every \(r\). Thus the only possible function is the identity.

Finally, if \(f(r)=r\), then the two sides of (1) are equal:
\[
n!+f(m)!=n!+m!=f(n)!+f(m!),
\]
so (1) is satisfied. Hence \(\boxed{f(n)=n}\).
